outline: Congenital disorders, including disease in adults
primary_competency: Medical Knowledge: Applying Foundational Science Concepts
diagnosis: Anomalous left coronary artery from the pulmonary artery (ALCAPA)
mechanism: In ALCAPA, the left coronary artery originates from the pulmonary artery rather than the aorta. Early after birth, relatively high pulmonary artery pressure can maintain some antegrade perfusion through the anomalous vessel. As pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressure fall, left-coronary perfusion pressure decreases and flow can reverse toward the low-pressure pulmonary artery; collateral flow from the right coronary system is then partly lost into the pulmonary artery (coronary steal), producing left-ventricular myocardial ischemia.
vignette: A 6-week-old infant is evaluated for recurrent episodes of intense crying, pallor, diaphoresis, and tachypnea during feeding. The infant was well during the first days after birth. Echocardiography shows left ventricular systolic dysfunction and mitral regurgitation. The left coronary artery arises from the main pulmonary artery rather than the aortic root.
lead: Which of the following postnatal hemodynamic changes most directly explains the development of this infant's myocardial ischemia?
correct: A fall in pulmonary vascular resistance lowers pulmonary artery pressure, promoting reduced antegrade and then retrograde flow through the anomalous left coronary artery into the pulmonary artery
distractors: The postnatal rise in systemic vascular resistance lowers aortic pressure and thereby reduces perfusion of the right coronary artery
Closure of the foramen ovale prevents oxygenated pulmonary venous blood from reaching the left ventricle and coronary circulation
The increase in left ventricular systolic pressure compresses the anomalous left coronary artery between the aorta and pulmonary trunk
A fall in pulmonary artery oxygen content causes ischemia while left-coronary flow remains antegrade and unchanged
distractor_notes: Systemic vascular resistance rises after placental separation, which increases rather than lowers systemic/aortic pressure. The defining hemodynamic problem in ALCAPA is the falling pulmonary arterial pressure and the resulting reduction/reversal of flow through the anomalous left coronary artery, not a postnatal fall in right-coronary perfusion pressure.

After birth, oxygenated pulmonary venous blood normally enters the left atrium and left ventricle directly; functional closure of the foramen ovale does not block this route. ALCAPA ischemia results from abnormal coronary origin and the changing pressure gradient between the coronary circulation and pulmonary artery.

Compression between the aorta and pulmonary trunk is a mechanism relevant to certain anomalous aortic coronary origins with an interarterial course. In ALCAPA, the left coronary artery originates from the pulmonary artery; the major mechanism is loss of pulmonary-artery perfusion pressure followed by coronary steal.

Pulmonary arterial oxygen content is not the sole determinant of perfusion in ALCAPA. The clinically important postnatal transition is the fall in pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressure, which reduces antegrade left-coronary perfusion and permits retrograde runoff into the lower-pressure pulmonary artery.
key_expl: The infant has ALCAPA. Immediately after birth, pulmonary artery pressure remains relatively high, so the anomalous left coronary artery can still receive some antegrade flow despite its desaturated source. As pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressure fall over the following weeks, perfusion pressure in the anomalous left coronary artery falls. Flow may reverse from right-coronary collaterals through the left coronary system into the lower-pressure pulmonary artery, creating a coronary-steal phenomenon and causing left-ventricular ischemia, dysfunction, and secondary mitral regurgitation.
objective: Explain why infants with ALCAPA often become symptomatic after an initially well neonatal period: the postnatal fall in pulmonary vascular resistance and pulmonary artery pressure reduces antegrade left-coronary perfusion and promotes retrograde coronary steal into the pulmonary artery.
clues: feeding-associated crying, pallor, diaphoresis, and tachypnea
left coronary artery arises from the main pulmonary artery
